title: Zack Polanski faces greatest crisis of his leadership so far
description: In the aftermath of a by-election, the focus is usually on the winner. Not this time.Make no mistake, the new MP for Holborn and St Pancras in north L
body: In the aftermath of a by-election, the focus is usually on the winner. Not this time.Make no mistake, the new MP for Holborn and St Pancras in north London, Sagal Abdi-Wali, has quite the story to tell.She arrived in the UK as a child refugee from Somalia in the 1990s, grew up locally in Camden, became a councillor four years ago, the council leader in May and is now Sir Keir Starmer's successor as the MP.But in the offices of Camden Council at three o'clock this morning, the focus of the press pack, me included, was on Zack Polanski, the leader of the Green Party of England and Wales, as we waited for the result.This constituency has long been a safe Labour seat – the political home of the former prime minister and before that the former cabinet minister Frank Dobson. So a Labour victory here falls in the column marked "relief" for Downing Street rather than "jubilation". Nonetheless, the Greens did very well in local elections in London in May, riding the crest of a political wave which began shortly after Polanski became the party's leader just over a year ago.His failure to win here will prompt questions from some about stalling momentum, but the party can and does point to the big swing to them since the general election and a result that was by a long way the second best ever result for them at a Westminster by-election.Incidentally, in finishing third the Conservatives have beaten Reform UK for the first time in an English by-election since the general election. It seems likely that Reform's result was hampered by Restore Britain, who managed almost half as many votes as Reform did, in a constituency not very favourable to either party.But the real reason for the nocturnal scramble of cameras, microphones and questions for Polanski had little to do with the by-election – and everything to do with a vote at the Green Party's conference in Brighton last weekend.Activists there passed a motion declaring Zionism as a form of racism.The motion defined Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backed a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.Polanski didn't take part in the vote because, he said, he chose to campaign in Holborn and St Pancras instead. And he repeatedly declined to do interviews, as the pressure on him as ratcheted up.But this morning he did speak to journalists.He told BBC Breakfast that if he had he been there for the vote he "would have voted for the amendments".Asked if he would have voted against the motion in the hall on that day, Polanski said: "the motion as amended I would have voted for, the motion unamended I wouldn't have voted for."He added:  "I think it's an imperfect motion, there's parts I disagree with and parts I agree with."Some in the party are furious about what has happened in recent days, with one figure telling me: "He has created a monster he either can't or won't control." Green Party membership has increased more than three fold in the last year and internal critics of Polanski say this includes hard-left campaigners focused on the Middle East rather than environmental concerns.Within the party and beyond it, a row is now boiling. Polanski, who is himself Jewish, has been banned from Israel. The Jewish Leadership Council and the Board of Deputies of British Jews have criticised the party, as have sister Green parties in Europe.And – significantly – the former party leader and one of the most important figures in the Green movement of her generation, Caroline Lucas, told BBC Newsnight Polanski had failed to show leadership over the issue. She also failed to back him carrying on as leader.Asked by reporters after the by-election result if he could continue as leader, Polanski insisted "of course I can carry on".He did not explicitly reject the motion his party has passed, saying there was an "ongoing genocide and the displacement of the Palestinian people". "I believe that is clearly racist," he added.Israel has repeatedly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide.And asked if he believed in a two-state solution – an Israeli and Palestinian state existing peacefully alongside each other – he said "I believe it is not our role to decide".He repeated that "it is my job to reassure people and make sure that we bring our party together". "No one will be excluded in the Green Party based on faith and religion," he said.But Polanski now confronts the greatest crisis of his leadership so far. He faces open, public insurrection about his judgement from senior figures internally and opprobrium from plenty of others beyond the party.The campaign in Holborn and St Pancras might be over. The questions for Polanski certainly aren't.

schema.headline: Zack Polanski faces greatest crisis of his leadership so far

title: Prize-winning image which sparked backlash was AI-generated, Nikon rules
description: The winner of a prestigious scientific photography competition has been disqualified following concerns raised by other scientists that it was fake.Ni
body: The winner of a prestigious scientific photography competition has been disqualified following concerns raised by other scientists that it was fake.Nikon said the use of generative AI in the composition of the video broke the rules of its Small World In Motion contest, which accepts photos and video taken using powerful microscopes.The firm said the video "did not comply with the competition rules regarding generative AI", but added it was not a judgement of the entrant's professional reputation or scientific contributions.It said it would now look at the rules and procedures of the annual contest, which has been running for 15 years and is specifically for microscopic images.Nikon said it came to the decision "after thoroughly re-evaluating the video and supporting materials and consulting with members of our judging panel".The winning entry came from Dr Ning Xu, from Tsinghua University in China, who submitted a short video showing tiny, hair-like structures called cilia moving in the airway of a child with the respiratory condition PCD.The BBC has approached him for comment.A number of scientists, including former competition judges, complained to Nikon on its LinkedIn page that the video did not appear to be real.Xu had acknowledged using AI, but said he believed he had acted within the rules, and had cooperated with Nikon's investigation.University of Leicester scientist Dr Robert Hirst, who was among the first experts to voice concerns, said he was "not surprised" and he "knew immediately that the video was fabricated"."I have been diagnosing PCD for 20 years by examining their cilia waveform, length, cell size and shape," he said.Hirst, who is lead scientist for the NHS centre for PCD diagnosis at the university, said the cells and cilia "look nothing like those from PCD patients"."This controversy has impacted a lot of patients, scientists, doctors and PCD support networks around the world," he said.

schema.headline: Prize-winning image which sparked backlash was AI-generated, Nikon rules

title: Nationwide cashier to repay £12k after stealing from customers
description: A building society cashier who stole thousands of pounds from customers to pay for "lavish" holidays has been ordered to repay more than £12,000.Kelly
body: A building society cashier who stole thousands of pounds from customers to pay for "lavish" holidays has been ordered to repay more than £12,000.Kelly Kershaw, 54, stole £13,333 including from vulnerable and elderly customers at Nationwide in Caernarfon, Gwynedd, even forging the signature of a man with learning disabilities.Kershaw admitted five counts of fraud after colleagues spotted Facebook posts of her on safari in Africa, and on trips to Paris, Tuscany and Dubai.She was jailed for 16 months in May but returned to Caernarfon Crown Court for a Proceeds of Crime Act, external hearing, and told to pay back £12,630.Judge Jones ordered Kershaw to repay the sum within three months or face a further five months in prison.The mother-of-two posted pictures of skiing trips, safaris and romantic European getaways on her Facebook page and boasted she was "living and loving life one adventure at a time."Kershaw's victims included an 85-year-old man who had lost some "cognitive abilities" after suffering a stroke - and she stole £6,300 from him.On one occasion, he came to the branch asking to withdraw £200, but Kershaw logged the withdrawal as £500 and pocketed £300 herself.Another victim was a 49-year-old man with learning difficulties who lost £1,400 to Kershaw - he had his bank card kept in the branch as he was a previous victim of fraud.

schema.headline: Nationwide cashier to repay £12k after stealing from customers

title: Lib Dem MP quits frontbench job over Ed Davey's leadership
description: Liberal Democrat MP Charlie Maynard has resigned from the party's frontbench and wants to see Sir Ed Davey replaced as leader.As first reported by the
body: Liberal Democrat MP Charlie Maynard has resigned from the party's frontbench and wants to see Sir Ed Davey replaced as leader.As first reported by the Financial Times, external, the Witney MP left his role as Treasury spokesman on Friday.Those close to Sir Ed privately acknowledge that there is what they see as a "small group" of Liberal Democrat MPs who are not happy with his leadership, of which Maynard is one.Daisy Cooper, the deputy leader of the party, said: "The vast majority of our MPs support Ed, want him to lead the party into the next election, and are furious at this distraction." The BBC has approached Maynard for comment. Lib Dem MP and former leader Tim Farron also defended Sir Ed, saying under his leadership the party was in a position to match or even beat the "record numbers of MPs" the party won at the last election. "To think we're helped by this kind of rubbish, you'd need to be smoking the kind of stuff even we aren't in favour of legalising," he quipped.Several other Lib Dem MPs, including some frontbenchers, also gave Davey their backing in social media posts on Friday evening. Julian Brazil, a Liberal Democrat council leader who has previously been critical of Sir Ed, said Maynard had "put his head above the parapet - we'll see if other people follow".Speaking to BBC Radio 5Live's Matt Chorley, he said: "I would have thought that in the next few days, we will see if there's a groundswell behind him."Brazil added that Sir Ed had been a "fantastic leader" but added: "For whatever reasons people aren't listening to Ed, they don't take notice of him, so we need to have a fresh start and be able to articulate what our vision of the country is."I think that's best done by someone else."Maynard was first elected to his Oxfordshire constituency in 2024, winning the traditionally Conservative seat, formerly held by David Cameron, with a majority of more than 4,000.Before becoming an MP, he ran an international mergers and acquisitions advisory firm. He is the second Lib Dem to leave the frontbench this week, following Alison Bennett's decision to resign her post of spokesperson for care and carers.Bennett would not confirmed why she stepped down but it is understood it was not for personal reasons. Under Liberal Democrat rules, a leadership contest can be triggered if a vote of no confidence in the leader is passed by the majority of all the party's MPs. To enter a leadership contest, a Lib Dem MP must have nominations from at least 10% of the parliamentary party, not including the candidate themselves, and have the backing of 200 members across at least 20 local parties. Sir Ed has been leader for six years and in the 2024 general election led the party to its biggest election success, winning 72 seats. However, the party has found it difficult to build on that success, with polling numbers remaining at relatively low levels. More recently, some Liberal Democrats have publicly attacked the leader for his stance on the triple lock - the mechanism which guarantees the state pension goes up each year in line with either inflation, wage increases, or 2.5% whichever is highest.Last week, Sir Ed criticised Andy Burnham's announcement that he would adjust the triple lock, arguing it would "put more pensioners into poverty". "This would mean people who are working hard now - the millennials - when they retire would have a very poor pension," he said. One Lib Dem MP described Sir Ed's argument as "nonsense", while another said: "Most millennials don't think there will be a state pension when they retire so this isn't being done with them in mind."

schema.headline: Lib Dem MP quits frontbench job over Ed Davey's leadership

title: Zack Polanski vows to stay as Green leader as he faces criticism after by-election defeat
description: Zack Polanski has vowed to stay on as Green Party leader after his by-election defeat, as he faced pressure from within his own party to resign.The le
body: Zack Polanski has vowed to stay on as Green Party leader after his by-election defeat, as he faced pressure from within his own party to resign.The leader of the Jewish Greens, Vivien Lichtenstein, said on Friday he should resign, adding it was a "big mistake" for him to have dodged a debate about a party conference motion that declared Zionism a form of racism.Lichtenstein's comments come after two former Green leaders accused Polanski of failing to show leadership over the Zionism row.Polanski, who came second to Labour overnight in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, told BBC Breakfast he would "absolutely" stay on as leader and "of course" had not questioned that.The Greens had hoped to take the seat, previously held by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, after a by-election success earlier this year.Polanski lost out in Thursday's contest in London to Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali, who secured 45% of the vote to his 33% - but the Green vote share was up by 22 percentage points on the 2024 general election.In her comments calling on Polanski to resign, Lichtenstein told Times Radio: "I don't know which Jewish members of the party he's been working with – it certainly hasn't been with the Jewish Greens committee."Her criticisms were similar to those of former Green Party leader Caroline Lucas who said Polanski should have attended the vote on the conference motion on Sunday.The motion, which was passed by rank-and-file members to become official party policy, defined Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backed a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.Adrian Ramsay, a Green MP and former co-leader, declined to back Polanski when asked on the BBC's Politics East on Friday."A lot depends on what happens in the days and weeks to come," he replied when asked if Polanski should still lead the party."[He] did not show leadership I would have been looking for," said Ramsay, who said he was now working to reverse the motion.Polanski defended his absence from the controversial motion vote in Brighton, saying he was busy campaigning in the North London constituency.Asked if he would resign, he said: "Of course I can carry on as leader of the Green Party."He added:  "Yes, I've taken a loss tonight but our movement is so much bigger than one election or one motion."Having not answered questions about the Zionism vote for most of this week, Polanski confirmed in interviews on Friday that he would not have voted for the "imperfect" motion without it being amended.However, he said "the displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people is clearly underpinned by a racist ideology".Several UN reports have accused the Israeli government of committing war crimes which amount to genocide in Gaza. Israel has repeatedly denied all such allegations.On Friday morning, following the Zionism row, Polanski was asked repeatedly on BBC Radio 4's Today programme whether he believes Israel has a right to exist."I don't believe any state has the right to oppress or to commit apartheid and certainly not genocide on another people," he said, adding: "I don't believe that's a state that anyone should be supporting."Asked by presenter Nick Robinson for a "yes/no" answer on this question, he said: "I've repeated many times that I want to see equal rights for Israelis and Palestinians - at the moment Palestinians don't have equal rights so I think I'm answering your question really clearly."But given his popularity among the grassroots, he may be safe from a leadership challenge in the near future.Former Green leader Caroline Lucas described the motion as "dangerous" and "flawed from top to bottom", and said leadership "was frankly missing" on it.She said she was not calling for Polanski to stand down and welcomed that he had "indicated he shares some of my concerns on the Zionism motion"."Now the party needs to come together to make the urgent changes needed to take us forward," she said.Jonathan Bartley, the Green co-leader from 2016 to 2021, called on Polanski to "put his hands up" and "say sorry" - but did not demand he quit."I think [the vote] was a failure of leadership from Zack and there is a certain toxicity now around the Green Party," he told BBC Radio 4's World at One.Bartley said the Green brand "needs to be detoxified", adding the party had seen an influx in members that have "maybe come from the left of the Labour Party, maybe from [Jeremy Corbyn's] Your Party" but "we're losing some older voters".The party's next scheduled leadership ballot takes place in summer 2027 - and Bartley said he thinks Polanski will face a challenger.Sian Berry, Green MP for Brighton Pavilion, said on Friday she was ready to work with colleagues "to restore trust in our processes and our party, fix the serious flaws in the motion that was passed" and build more inclusive policies.The Green leader has faced days of pressure over the Zionism motion. Four of the five Green MPs and one of the party's two deputy leaders opposed it, the Green deputy in Wales and some councillors resigned, while some local members and the European Green Party have distanced themselves from it.Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called on Polanski to reverse the "completely wrong" motion.Meanwhile, Labour chair Bridget Phillipson drew comparisons with her party's previous antisemitism scandal, telling the BBC she felt the Greens now face a "serious problem" with antisemitism.Polanski has said anti-Zionism and antisemitism are distinct from each other and said nobody will be excluded from the party on the basis of their faith, place of worship or religious body.

schema.headline: Zack Polanski vows to stay as Green leader as he faces criticism after by-election defeat

title: Russian search engine Yandex struggles after Ukrainian strikes on data centres
description: Russian tech giant Yandex has said it was struggling to maintain services after two of its five data centres were struck by Ukrainian drones in the pa
body: Russian tech giant Yandex has said it was struggling to maintain services after two of its five data centres were struck by Ukrainian drones in the past two days.Often dubbed "Russia's Google", the company runs the country's most popular search engine, as well as a food-ordering and taxi app used by tens of millions of people.President Volodymyr Zelensky said the attacks were in response to weeks of Russian strikes on Ukrainian data centres.Both sides have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months as the war between the two drags on. Kyiv says its strikes are aimed at revenue streams for Moscow's war machine, and that the latest attacks could force Russia to divert resources to Yandex.Yandex said that its data centre in Sasovo, in the Ryazan region, had been "seriously damaged as a result of a drone attack" overnight into Thursday, with its operations "completely suspended".Another data centre in Kaluga, a region south-west of Moscow, had also been attacked on Friday morning, it said, with part of that site's infrastructure "taken out of service".Yandex said on Friday that its data centres were "critical" for the normal operation of its services and that it was "very difficult to predict" when they would be back online.It said teams were working "day and night" to keep services running, but "unfortunately it is not a simple task".The tech giant said none of its employees had been injured in the strikes. The regional governor in Kaluga said nine people had been injured in a drone attack on the city's infrastructure.The exact scope of the disruption to the company's services is unclear - though it told state news agency Tass that some of its AI chatbot functions were temporarily unavailable, while its smart home devices may also experience problems.Yandex previously said its Kaluga data centre was one of Russia's largest - covering an area of 130,000 sqm (1,399,000 sq ft) and consuming as much electricity annually as 220,000 UK households.Its data centre in Sasovo, meanwhile, houses two of three supercomputers used to develop the company's AI model. It is unclear whether the supercomputers survived the attack.Ukraine's defence ministry confirmed the data centre attacks, saying they could "force Russia to divert resources to repair the damaged capacity".Zelensky said Kyiv was responding to similar Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centres in a "mirror-like fashion".Last month, a Russian drone hit a business centre in Kyiv, killing four people and damaging a data centre. Due to the strikes, about 100,000 households in Kyiv and the region suffered internet outages.Some Ukrainian firms have already begun moving data from damaged servers to facilities abroad.Moscow has justified the attacks by saying the data centres were used by Ukrainian military intelligence.But Ukraine accuses it of deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure. Russia has stepped up strikes on energy infrastructure ahead of the winter, as it has done in previous years of the full-scale invasion, which began in 2022.

schema.headline: Russian search engine Yandex struggles after Ukrainian strikes on data centres

title: Fort Hood survivor supports gunman's execution by firing squad but questions livestream
description: A former US Army sergeant who survived the mass shooting at the Fort Hood base has said that while he supported the execution of the gunman by firing
body: A former US Army sergeant who survived the mass shooting at the Fort Hood base has said that while he supported the execution of the gunman by firing squad, he was concerned about it being livestreamed.Alonzo Lunsford, who was shot seven times, told the BBC that the "method is befitting" for Nidal Hasan's execution because other methods like lethal injection would be "doing him a favour".Hasan, then a US Army psychiatrist, fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers in a medical building at Fort Hood, in Texas, in 2009. But while Lunsford agreed with the method of execution, he said it was "not something you should view for entertainment purposes".He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday: "To show the whole thing without it being censored for the general public, for me personally, I don't agree with that, but it's not about my personal belief."US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said the public will be able to view a livestream of the execution, saying it was important for people to see the consequences of this kind of crime. If it goes ahead - and legal experts told the BBC it might not ever happen - it would be the first public execution in the US in almost a century.Lunsford explained that while he was concerned about the "effect" and "message" a livestream would send to younger people, when it comes to the survivors, their families and the families of the victims, they "should be able to look at it"."I'm gonna be there [to watch in person] and before they pull the trigger, I want him to look at me in my eyes and I look at him in his eyes and I want him to know: 'Dude you failed, I'm still here,'" he said."I don't really have any sympathy for him as far as firing squad vs lethal injection, hanging or gas chamber, because he didn't have that same compassion when he did the deed on 5 November," the former sergeant explained. "I think the method is befitting for him because the lethal injection - that's doing him a favour. Gas chamber? Is doing him a favour."But Lunsford said that, as a Christian, he had forgiven Hasan because "I cannot heal if I don't forgive him"."We're taught that with your last breath you can ask for forgiveness and I think that's what he [Hasan] should do," he added.Telling his account of what happened that day, he said Hasan got out of his chair and jumped onto a counter, before pulling out a weapon and discharging it.Lunsford said he had been looking for an exit via the back door, which was "two or three strides" away from him when he was first shot above his left eye and then "hit two more times in my back" as he crawled behind a desk."At that point I played dead," he said. When Hasan moved on, Lunsford grabbed a nearby wounded soldier and went outside, where he said Hasan came up behind them and shot him again.One memory he said that "bothers" him from the day was of a woman who told Hasan she was pregnant."We heard a gunshot and the last thing that girl was saying was: 'Oh my god, my baby, my baby.'"Lunsford said personnel did not carry weapons in medical facilities and that Hasan "took the coward's way out" to attack them there."And then for him to say he is fighting for his cause? I've read the Quran and everything that he said he was doing that was in the Quran is not supported by the Quran," he explained.Hasan's execution was announced by the Pentagon earlier this week, in what will be the first military execution in more than 60 years.Legal experts have told the BBC there are a number of hurdles around the livestreaming of this which could mean it is successfully challenged in court.Some politicians have been vocal in their opposition.Democratic Senator Chris Murphy told CNN it was "disgusting" while Republican Senator Thom Tillis said public executions were what "oppressive dictators" did."It should not be happening in America," he added in a post on X., external

schema.headline: Fort Hood survivor supports gunman's execution by firing squad but questions livestream

title: Fort Hood attacker's execution by firing squad will be livestreamed, Pentagon says
description: The public will be able to watch the execution of a former US Army major by firing squad, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has said.A Defence Departm
body: The public will be able to watch the execution of a former US Army major by firing squad, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has said.A Defence Department official told the BBC the execution of Nidal Hasan, who fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers at the Fort Hood military base in 2009, would be livestreamed.It is believed it would be the first public execution in the US in almost a century. The decision to livestream it was "unprecedented in the modern era" and "on uncertain legal terrain", said John Mills, a lawyer who works with inmates sentenced to death. "People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," said Hegseth. The UN human rights office told AFP that livestreaming it would be "tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture".Democratic Senator Chris Murphy told CNN that the idea was "disgusting" and reminiscent of executions carried out by the Islamic State group.The Pentagon announced earlier this week it would execute Hasan in the first military execution in more than 60 years.Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist from Virginia, admitted fatally shooting 13 unarmed soldiers in a crowded medical building at Fort Hood.Alonzo Lunsford, a former US Army sergeant who was shot seven times in the attack, told the BBC's Today programme that he supported the execution by firing squad, as a method "befitting" for what he did.But he said he did not believe everyone should be able to watch the livestream over concerns about the message it might send to younger people, but added that it was important that those affected by the shooting were given the opportunity."As far as the families of the fallen and the families of the survivors, and the survivors themselves, yes, I think we should be able to look at it uncensored."Lunsford said he planned to attend the execution and before they pull the trigger he wants Hasan to look him in the eyes. "I want him to know he failed. I'm still here." Hegseth said in an interview with conservative TV outlet Real America's Voice that Hasan was "gonna get a firing squad of soldiers - as it should be".Asked whether Hasan had made any final requests or reached out to US President Donald Trump, Hegseth said: "Don't care. We'll see him on December 3rd."A Pentagon spokesperson said on Monday that Trump had approved the defence secretary's recommendation. The BBC has asked the White House whether Trump supported a livestreamed public execution.Trump said on Friday that he believed Hasan deserved the execution by firing squad, but he did not mention the livestreaming.Speaking at an event ahead of a federal holiday celebrating Christopher Columbus that was first observed in 1937, the president said that in the 1900s "we had really strong laws."   He then said that today "you can do almost anything. Nothing happens. But we're changing that." While there were more than 2,700 executions across 17 countries last year, only two nations carried them out publicly. Eleven public executions were known to have been carried out in Iran in 2025 and another six in Afghanistan, according to Amnesty International.The US Conference of Catholic Bishops condemned the decision to publicly livestream Hasan's execution, expressing "shock and great sorrow" in a statement."Our God is the God of life," Archbishop and conference president Paul Coakley said. "In no way can Hassan's actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered."The execution is scheduled to take place at Fort Hood in Texas on 3 December. It will be the first military execution by firing squad since the end of World War Two.In court, Hasan apologised for "any mistakes". He said during his court martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan.A military execution requires approval from the US president, according to military law. It also requires appellate review, when a higher court inspects the decision and gives a final judgement on its legality to move forward.The appellate process for Hasan was not over, Mills said, and he was likely to seek a review of his conviction and sentence in federal court, which would likely stay the execution. As such, Mills said that he would be surprised if the execution happened."Seeking to make it livestreamed, a firing squad execution, is little more than attention-seeking by the Trump administration and is unlikely to occur, much less deliver any semblance of justice," he added.Certain states require some form of public viewing of executions. Many states require journalists to be present and the person due to be executed can also invite people. Others allow ordinary citizens to volunteer as witnesses.But "there hasn't ever been a livestreamed execution", said Deborah Denno, who has studied US execution methods.A livestreamed execution would "force a level of transparency that we have probably never seen before in this country", the Fordham University law professor said. "More than half of the country wants the death penalty - even though that's on the decline - [and] an argument could be made that 'if you want the death penalty, then we are going to show you how it's conducted in this country'," she said."And people would have to realise exactly what's happening in a way that many people ignore."Denno said there were important considerations for a livestream, such as whether it would be age-restricted.Only certain categories of people, such as journalists and relatives, are permitted to watch military executions under Army Regulation 190-55, external. People aged under 18 are excluded.The BBC has asked the Pentagon and US Army whether the rules restricting who can watch will be waived and what safeguards will be in place to stop young people from watching the stream.A Defence Department official told the BBC that more details on the livestreamed execution would follow.The countries with the highest number of executions last year were China, Iran, Saudi Arabia, Yemen and the US, in that order, Amnesty International data shows.Trump overturned his predecessor Joe Biden's moratorium on federal executions when he returned to the White House.Two thirds of Americans (66%) support executions of murderers, a figure which has risen six points in the last five years, according to a Pew Research survey conducted in July, external.The last military execution in the country took place in 1961, when a US Army private was hanged after being convicted of raping an 11-year-old Austrian girl. The execution was authorised by then-President Dwight D Eisenhower and took place despite the victim's family asking his successor, John F Kennedy, for clemency.The last military execution by firing squad took place in January 1945, when a young US Army deserter, Eddie Slovik, was shot during the final months of WW2.Additional reporting by Kwasi Gyamfi Asiedu and Kali Hays

schema.headline: Fort Hood attacker's execution by firing squad will be livestreamed, Pentagon says

title: Dad and son remain critical after masked men attack in Leicestershire village
description: Image source, Leicester Media OnlineImage caption, Officers were called to reports of a disturbance in Thurnby on ThursdayByDan HuntEast MidlandsUpdat
body: Image source, Leicester Media OnlineImage caption, Officers were called to reports of a disturbance in Thurnby on ThursdayByDan HuntEast MidlandsUpdated 2 hours agoA father and son are in hospital in a life-threatening condition after an attack in their family home which appeared "completely unprovoked", police have said.Officers were called to reports of a disturbance at a house in Station Road, Thurnby, shortly before 00:30 BST on Thursday.Leicestershire Police said a man in his 50s was stabbed multiple times, while a boy, 15, was also stabbed by two masked men who entered the property. The force gave an update on Friday to say both remained critical in hospital.Officers added that the man's wife - who is in her 40s - suffered minor injuries to her hand and shoulder during the attack. Three other children who were in the address were not injured.In the interest of public and police safety, police said armed officers were deployed but the men had left the house prior to them arriving.The force added an investigation, led by the East Midlands Special Operations Unit (EMSOU), to understand the circumstances and motive would continue over the weekend.Image caption, Police have urged the public to come forward with any information about the attackPolice said it would remain in the area as officers undertook searches for anything that may help them to understand and identify those responsible.Det Insp Lorna Granville said: "This was a violent attack against a family in their own home which appears to have been completely unprovoked."Our investigation to understand what happened and why - and identify those behind such a horrific criminal act - is going to continue over the weekend."I'm making a direct appeal to people in Thurnby and the surrounding communities to come forward with any information if they haven't already done so. "We owe it to the victims to locate the perpetrators and bring them to justice."Image source, Leicester Media OnlineImage caption, One of the forensic officers at the scene on ThursdayGranville added: "I'd like to speak to anyone who may have seen or heard anything suspicious, unusual or untoward in the area of Station Road and Somerby Road between 23:00 on Wednesday and the early hours of yesterday morning."This includes anyone who was driving in the area and captured anything on a dashcam or anyone with CCTV or doorbell footage."Anything you're able to provide, no matter how insignificant you think it might be, could help us."The force said it had set up a major incident public portal for the public to submit information.Simon Galton, councillor for Thurnby and Houghton, said he was "absolutely appalled" to hear of the attack on Thursday."Thurnby is a quiet place, yes we have anti-social behaviour, but we don't have serious violent crime of this nature."It's quite unprecedented in Thurnby."Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Leicester

schema.headline: Dad and son remain critical after masked men attack in Leicestershire village

title: Drumcree: Boutcher asks secretary of state to review Parades Commission ruling
description: Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) Chief Constable Jon Boutcher has asked the secretary of state to review the Parades Commission determination
body: Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) Chief Constable Jon Boutcher has asked the secretary of state to review the Parades Commission determination allowing the Drumcree parade, BBC  News NI understands.Boutcher triggered the move under the Public Processions (Northern Ireland) Act 1998 earlier on Friday.It comes as First Minister Michelle O'Neill confirmed she has received a letter from police investigating protests over the Drumcree parading dispute.Portadown deputy District Master Alastair Power said there would be "serious consequences" if the Northern Ireland secretary intervened to stop the march.It is the 13th day of deadlock between residents of the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road and the local district lodge of the Orange Order.The Parades Commission ruled that the march could go ahead with restrictions in place.But the parade, from Drumcree Church into Portadown, did not happen due to a large protest on the Garvaghy Road.On Thursday, the police said they had begun issuing letters inviting people "reasonably suspected" of committing offences linked to the protests to interview.Unionist politicians have called for action to be taken against O'Neill and other senior Sinn Féin politicians who took part in the protests against the Orange Order march down the Garvaghy Road at the end of last month.Under section nine of the Public Processions (Northern Ireland) Act 1998, Boutcher can make an application asking Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant to reconsider the Parades' Commission determination.Neither the PSNI nor the Northern Ireland Office (NIO) has commented on the development.But BBC NI understands Bryant is now in the process of consulting with Boutcher and the commission.Sources state he has not yet reached any conclusion.Under the legislation, the minister has the power to revoke a determination, amend it, or stick by it.Meanwhile, in a statement issued by Sinn Féin on Friday afternoon, O'Neill confirmed she had received a letter from the PSNI. "I can confirm I have received a letter inviting me for a police interview in relation to a peaceful protest on the Garvaghy Road. I will co-operate with the investigation," O'Neill said. "For the last two weeks, I have stood in solidarity with the Garvaghy Road residents as attempts were made to force an unwanted Orange march through their community," she said. "I will continue to stand with the Garvaghy Road residents who should be allowed to live in peace and free from sectarian intimidation," she added. The police statement did not name anyone they planned to issue a letter to.Earlier, Sinn Féin President Mary Lou McDonald said the party would "cooperate" in every way it could but that they remained "comfortable" in standing up for Garvaghy Road residents.Sinn Féin MLA Deirdre Hargey also told the BBC that she had received a letter and would seek legal advice.Loyalist activist Jamie Bryson held a press conference on Friday, alongside DUP MP Carla Lockhart.He said he had personal details published online on Thursday. "I have received over 1,500 abusive calls, over 280 voicemails, many with threats to kill, to murder me, my family, people around me, and things have just reached a level now where it's totally unacceptable," he said.Lockhart appealed to people to "step back" from making threats to her and Bryson.She said: "People can fight us on our politics and our policies, and they may not like what we say and I'll take anyone on with regards to my politics."But when it gets personal and when you see and hear these threats online all it takes is for one person to just seriously think 'I really don't like those people' and I firmly believe it's getting to that point."

schema.headline: Drumcree: Boutcher asks secretary of state to review Parades Commission ruling

title: Fury vs Joshua: Tickets priced up to £13,000 for all-British showdown sell out in one hour
description: Tickets for Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua's fight at Cardiff's Principality Stadium have sold out in just one hour.Fury and Joshua will meet on a bill
body: Tickets for Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua's fight at Cardiff's Principality Stadium have sold out in just one hour.Fury and Joshua will meet on a bill that begins on 11 December but they are not expected to fight until the early hours of 12 December.The highest-priced tickets were available at £13,128, including booking fees, with the lowest at £88.50.The all-British heavyweight contest, which will be broadcast globally on Netflix, was announced in September and around 80,000 tickets went on sale at 12:00 BST on Friday.Just minutes after the tickets went on sale more than 500,000 people were waiting in the online queue.Tickets quickly began emerging on resale websites, with ringside VIP seats being advertised for £73,645, while upper tier seats were available for £425.Ringwalks are expected to start around 01:00 GMT on Saturday 12 December, following a short live music performance, and the stadium will remain open until 03:30.The event is being promoted as a collaboration between Saudi boxing powerbroker Turki Alalshikh's The Ring and UFC chief Dana White.Organisers are yet to confirm any of the undercard fights.

schema.headline: Fury vs Joshua: Tickets priced up to £13,000 for all-British showdown sell out in one hour

title: Two men bailed after security breach at RAF Molesworth
description: Two Latvian men arrested after a fence was breached at a Cambridgeshire RAF base have been bailed.Ministry of Defence Police (MDP) security patrols at
body: Two Latvian men arrested after a fence was breached at a Cambridgeshire RAF base have been bailed.Ministry of Defence Police (MDP) security patrols at RAF Molesworth, which is used by the US military and Nato for intelligence operations, identified an abandoned vehicle at about 22:00 BST on Wednesday. The pair, aged 36 and 32 and who live in the UK, were subsequently arrested inside the perimeter a few hours after searches found a small breach of the fence at the site.Both were taken to a Cambridgeshire police station and have since been bailed with "strict conditions", the Metropolitan Police said.The force's Counter Terrorism Policing London is investigating.Its head Cdr Helen Flanagan said: "We're very aware of the recent heightened interest and concern around military sites, but there is nothing from our investigation so far to suggest this incident is connected to the events at RAF Fairford last week."Both men were initially arrested on suspicion of trespass on a prohibited site and criminal damage - after Cambridgeshire Police officers joined the search - and were taken to a local station.They were later arrested on suspicion of namely entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK under Section 4 of the National Security Act.

schema.headline: Two men bailed after security breach at RAF Molesworth

title: Singapore Grand Prix: Max Verstappen beats George Russell to Singapore sprint pole
description: The settings issue in Singapore, which was combined with a glitch in the F1 timing system that delayed the start of second qualifying, affected all ca
body: The settings issue in Singapore, which was combined with a glitch in the F1 timing system that delayed the start of second qualifying, affected all cars but had a bigger impact on some drivers than others, depending on the timing of their runs.The problem involved the settings being different before and after a red flag caused by a crash for Sergio Perez's Cadillac and left drivers complaining of reduced power.It involved overtake mode - which allows an extra 0.5MJ of energy to be harvested - being switched on and off again in the space of 28 seconds.Williams driver Carlos Sainz was knocked out in the first session after what we described as a "really poor lap", but added: "On top of that, half the cars did the lap with half a second quicker engine than the others. "There was another software issue and we were on the bad end of it, and for whatever reason, the FIA, like in Malaysia, again didn't decide to do sporting equity and were happy to do half of the quali with cars with higher power than the other half of the cars."A bit confused why the sport keeps doing different things depending on who is out in Q1 or who is out in lap one."Sainz said he did not think he would have made it through even without the settings problem.Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad and Aston Martin's Lance Stroll were other drivers who were affected and were knocked out in the first session. Stroll's team-mate Fernando Alonso also suffered, but did progress, eventually qualifying 15th.The FIA said in a statement: "During the first period of sprint qualifying there was a human error in race control unrelated to the timing issue also encountered in SQ1."This issue in question meant overtake mode was not available after the red flag period during SQ1."When it became apparent that overtake mode was not active after the restart, it was then activated for a period of 27 seconds before being deactivated again."The FIA acknowledges that this unfortunate human error had an impact on the performance of certain cars based on the timing of their run and their position around the lap."The second and third periods of sprint qualifying were not affected."The FIA system automatically disables overtake mode when there is a red flag. A pop-up then appears on the screen asking whether officials want to re-enable it.This was ignored, then overtake mode was reactivated before being disabled again, on the basis that it was fairer to do so than leave it enabled.Verstappen's pole lap appeared to be further confirmation of Red Bull's resurgence after his dominant win in Malaysia.He faced an investigation for overtaking Hamilton under yellow flags shown before the first session was stopped for the Perez incident, but officials took no further action.The four-time champion said he had not believed pole was possible before qualifying."We have some difficulties with the car in ride, as we know," he said, "but at least when we went to the soft tyres (in the final session), it made the car a bit more stable in places where before you were a bit unsure."I did not expect this but you take it, I'm happy for sure. Qualifying tomorrow is still the main goal and for us the start is always a critical point but at least a positive end to our day."Russell's performance compared with that of Antonelli raises further doubts about the efficacy of the Mercedes upgrade introduced in Malaysia.It was their biggest car update since the Canadian Grand Prix in May but team boss Toto Wolff said at Sepang that it had appeared to take them backwards rather than forwards.Mercedes split the car spec here in Singapore in an attempt to better understand its performance but Antonelli ended the session 0.573secs behind Russell.The Briton said: "As a team there is still nothing telling us it isn't working but it's all driven by the stopwatch and, yeah, the stopwatch hasn't been great for the upgrade yet. Maybe tomorrow's a different day."Antonelli, who leads the championship by 84 points going into the weekend, said: "Already FP1 I was struggling and there is still a lot to understand about this package. Really the car is very difficult, very unpredictable, very difficult to put a lap together. It's a shame. I was coming with high hopes but so far it has been very difficult."It's going to be a difficult weekend unless we can pull something out tomorrow. Other than that it is going very tricky. I don't really see where we can find 0.7secs but you never know."Wolff said before sprint qualifying: "The new car seems to be a little more tricky to drive. Not saying it's necessarily slower, because there will be goodness in it, but maybe we haven't just found a way of putting it all together and tuning it. The older car is a bit more stable, grippy, but that is really just one data point."Leclerc was 0.243secs off pole, and ruing what he said was Ferrari "losing a little bit of our raw performance" in the past three or four races.However, he added: "Still I feel there is potential in the car and maybe tomorrow we can be there or thereabouts in fighting for pole."Hamilton said: "We did a slightly different run plan to the others. It was my choice, but I think we got that wrong. But ultimately, the car was very oversteery on that lap. If the rears [tyres] are not ready or they are overheating, it's difficult to say. But it was very snappy and oversteery in the lap overall."

schema.headline: Singapore Grand Prix: Max Verstappen beats George Russell to Singapore sprint pole

title: US unveils sanctions on ICC in move court condems as 'assault on rule of law'
description: The Trump administration has unveiled sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) in a significant acceleration of its attempt to "di
body: The Trump administration has unveiled sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) in a significant acceleration of its attempt to "dismantle" what it sees as a "rogue" institution.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the measures - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans.The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order.The announcement came just hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law.The US has already sanctioned 17 of the ICC's judges and officials, but this move sanctions the court itself as an institution and is intended to collapse its ability to operate financially.However, the US has provided a six month grace period before some of these latest sanctions kick in, meaning member states can keep paying for its operations - a move Washington says is to allow countries time to negotiate a "solution to address" US concerns.UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres called the US decision "a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar".The UK joined Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan and the Netherlands in reaffirming their "continued and unwavering support" for the ICC and said they "regret and strongly disagree with" the sanctions.They also praised the court's staff for their work bringing "those accused of the most serious international crimes to justice", as well as supporting victims.The ICC was founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide, and counts 125 countries as member states. Several major countries remain outside the ICC, including the US, Russia, China, India and Israel.The Trump administration argues the ICC is run by what it calls globalists who threaten American sovereignty. It is furious over a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan the court has since closed and by its arrest warrants for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The new sanctions, however, do not say that those warrants must be withdrawn before the measures can be lifted.But Rubio said Trump would not allow the ICC to prosecute Americans, adding: "Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC."The US sanctions will stop US companies from providing goods or services to the ICC, such as banking or software.Rubio said Washington had delayed imposing the sanctions in the hope that the ICC and its member countries would address US concerns. He said the measures had been structured to allow other countries to negotiate a possible solution.He also called on US allies that were ICC signatories, including the UK, to "rein in" the institution.The Netherlands, which hosts the court in The Hague and is also a Nato ally of the US, faces particular pressure. Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen has said the sanctions would seriously affect the court's ability to function.Netanyahu welcomed the sanctions, saying the ICC was "not a court" but a political body that threatened law-abiding democracies and "the very idea of national sovereignty".The ICC said that the sanctions were aimed at disrupting its work and intimidating those who co-operate with it - but that it "will not be deterred".It called the measures "an assault on the rule of law" and said no one should be punished for serving the cause of justice, adding: "History will judge this moment."This showdown potentially marks the gravest crisis in the court's 24-year history. Rather than targeting individual ICC judges and prosecutors, the US is now sanctioning the court itself.

schema.headline: US unveils sanctions on ICC in move court condems as 'assault on rule of law'
